The Blue Marble is a famous photograph of the Earth taken by the Apollo 17 crew on December 7, 1972. It is one of the most iconic and enduring images of our planet. The photograph was captured by astronaut Harrison Schmitt, who was part of the Apollo 17 mission, the last manned mission to the Moon.

The image shows the Earth as a blue and white marble suspended in the blackness of space, with the sun's light reflecting off the oceans and clouds. The photograph was taken from a distance of about 29,000 kilometers (18,000 miles) away from the Earth, using a 70mm Hasselblad camera.

The Blue Marble image has become a powerful symbol of our planet and its fragility. It has been widely used in environmental and scientific contexts to raise awareness about the importance of protecting the Earth and its resources. The image has also been used in various forms of media, including posters, books, and even as a logo for environmental organizations.

The Blue Marble image has also been updated over the years, with new versions taken by satellites and spacecraft. However, the original 1972 image remains the most iconic and widely recognized representation of our planet.

Interestingly, the Blue Marble image was not the first photograph of the Earth from space, but it was the first to show the entire planet in a single frame. The image has had a profound impact on our understanding of the Earth and its place in the universe, and it continues to inspire new generations of scientists, environmentalists, and space enthusiasts.
